frameworks.name: Value Equation (100M Offers Framework)
frameworks.definition: Four variables that drive perceived value and purchasing decisions: Dream Outcome, Perceived Likelihood of Achievement, Time Delay (speed of delivery), and Effort and Sacrifice (friction of use). Maximize Dream Outcome and Likelihood; minimize Time Delay and Effort.

frameworks.name: Value Enhancers (Urgency, Scarcity, Guarantees, Bonuses, Naming)
frameworks.definition: Five offer-design levers that sit on top of the core Value Equation to further increase purchasing propensity; each lever independently raises perceived value or lowers perceived risk.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the four-variable Value Equation from his book $100 Million Offers applies equally to physical e-commerce products and service businesses, because the variables driving purchasing decisions (Dream Outcome, Perceived Likelihood of Achievement, Time Delay, and Effort/Sacrifice) are universal to any commercial transaction where a buyer values the outcome more than the price tag.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to B2B and B2C services
claims.mechanism: Customers buy when subjective value exceeds price; the four variables are the levers that constitute subjective value regardless of delivery format.
bounded_by: Application mechanics differ between services and physical products even though underlying variables are the same

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the Dream Outcome variable in offer design requires avatar-specific messaging: a buyer who wants a warm jacket and a buyer who wants a fashionable jacket represent different dream outcomes for the same physical product, and conflating them in a single message reduces conversion because the offer does not speak to the specific job-to-be-done.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical product with multiple use cases or buyer segments
claims.mechanism: Each distinct dream outcome maps to a distinct avatar whose purchase decision is driven by that specific outcome; a message optimized for one outcome actively fails to resonate with buyers seeking the other.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that product reviews on a listing page increase Perceived Likelihood of Achievement for buyers, which directly lifts conversion rates, because reading that other buyers achieved the desired outcome makes a prospective buyer more confident they will too. He credits Amazon as the pioneer of review infrastructure for exactly this mechanism.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Seeing other buyers report success with the product reduces uncertainty about personal outcome, raising the buyer's subjective probability of getting what they want.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that short how-to demonstration videos (e.g., 90-second styling guides) attached to a product listing increase a buyer's Perceived Likelihood of Achievement by giving them a concrete mental model of how to use the product successfully. He cites a Levi's jean jacket ad showing three ways to style the jacket as an example he described as 'masterful' in execution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical product where buyer uncertainty is about how to use or wear it, not about product quality
claims.mechanism: Demonstrating the specific behavior required to achieve the desired outcome eliminates the buyer's uncertainty about their own competence, which is the primary barrier when the product itself is credible but the buyer doubts their ability to use it.

numbers.axis: video length for how-to product demonstration

bounded_by: Less applicable when buyer uncertainty is about product quality rather than usage competence

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that Amazon's sustained competitive investment in compressing delivery time from two-day to one-day to one-hour shipping reflects the principle that faster delivery (shorter Time Delay between purchase and possession) directly increases the perceived value of the same product and drives repeat purchasing on the platform.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical product e-commerce where the product itself is consumed or used immediately after receipt
claims.mechanism: The closer to zero the gap between desire and gratification, the higher the subjective value; Amazon invests in delivery speed because it is a direct lever on customer lifetime value and platform stickiness.

numbers.axis: Amazon Prime delivery speed over time

bounded_by: Custom-tailored or made-to-order products have a different time delay structure where speed of production, not just shipping, is the lever

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that one-click checkout technology (e.g., Amazon's stored card, Bolt, ShopPay) increases e-commerce sales by reducing the Effort and Sacrifice associated with the purchase decision, making the same product more valuable in a real economic sense.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: digital checkout context for physical products
claims.mechanism: Friction in the checkout flow is a real cost imposed on the buyer; removing that friction is equivalent to adding value, which increases the likelihood of purchase completion.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that Amazon's in-stock quantity display (e.g., 'Only 2 left', 'Only 6 left', broken down by size) functions as a scarcity signal that drives conversion by creating urgency around inventory depletion, and that e-commerce operators can replicate this tactic at any scale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Visible inventory limits activate loss aversion in the buyer: the prospect of not being able to purchase later increases present purchase intent.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that Amazon's Lightning Deals (price discount valid for 60 minutes) function as pure urgency, and that limited-edition product drops (e.g., 100 t-shirts released at a specific hour, first come first served) combine scarcity with urgency, both of which are distinct levers in the Value Equation framework that increase conversion when applied to e-commerce.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

anchors.value: 100 units, first-come-first-served at a fixed drop time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that Amazon's 'try before you buy' (7-day trial with delayed billing) functions as a second-layer guarantee on top of the standard money-back guarantee, and that this layered guarantee structure reduces purchase risk to near zero, thereby increasing Perceived Likelihood of Achievement by allowing the customer to validate the outcome before paying.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical product e-commerce where fit or feel is a primary purchase barrier (e.g., apparel)
claims.mechanism: If the buyer can validate the outcome before committing payment, their perceived likelihood of a positive experience is near certain at the moment of payment decision, removing the psychological cost of purchase risk.
bounded_by: Money-back guarantee has become table stakes for physical products and on its own no longer differentiates

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for supplement and home-goods e-commerce products, usage-instruction bonuses (how to take the product, what to combine it with, optimal timing, adherence tips) are a legitimate value-adding component that increases Perceived Likelihood of Achievement and reduces churn, not merely a marketing add-on.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: consumable or complex physical products where correct usage materially affects outcome
e.g. supplements, home-health devices, kitchen appliances
bounded_by: Bonus content adds less value for products where use is self-evident (e.g., a standard garment with no styling complexity)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that naming a product in a way that states the dream outcome explicitly (e.g., including 'warm', 'hot', 'fire' in a cold-weather jacket name, vs. 'light fashion' in a style-only jacket name) increases conversion by signaling to the buyer that this product is specifically the solution to their stated job-to-be-done.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical product in a category where multiple sub-outcomes exist for the same product type (e.g., jackets: warm vs. fashionable)
claims.mechanism: An outcome-explicit product name functions as a pre-filter: the buyer whose dream outcome matches the name self-selects in, perceiving high congruence between their need and the product, reducing the cognitive work required to buy.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that an e-commerce operator who implements the full Value Equation stack (higher Perceived Likelihood via reviews and demos, compressed Time Delay via fast shipping, reduced Effort via one-click checkout, plus all five enhancers: scarcity, urgency, guarantees, bonuses, and outcome-explicit naming) will outperform a competitor with the same physical product who has implemented none of these, despite having identical products.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: two e-commerce operators selling identical physical products
claims.mechanism: Perceived value, not product quality, is the primary determinant of purchase likelihood; all value-equation variables are under operator control independently of the product itself.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that unboxing videos reduce the perceived risk of purchasing a physical product online by demystifying the post-purchase experience, because they give the buyer concrete expectations that the product will meet, which increases their willingness to buy by reducing the uncertainty about what happens after payment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: physical product purchase online where tangibility uncertainty is a barrier
claims.mechanism: Uncertainty about the post-purchase experience (what arrives, what it looks like, what happens when you open it) is a real purchase barrier; unboxing content collapses that uncertainty, converting a vague risk into a concrete known, making purchase psychologically safer.

examples.text: Levi's ran a roughly 90-second video ad for a jean jacket showing three distinct ways to style it: paired with dark clothing, paired with light clothing, and worn double-denim with matching jeans. Alex Hormozi cited this as a masterful execution of Perceived Likelihood of Achievement: a buyer who did not know how to style a jean jacket now has a concrete mental model, raising their confidence that they will achieve the 'look cool' dream outcome they sought.

Amazon's Prime delivery program illustrates the Time Delay variable of the Value Equation in e-commerce. Originally offering 2-day delivery, Amazon progressively reduced this to 1-day and then 1-hour delivery in select markets, explicitly investing in speed because they understood that faster delivery increased the perceived value of every item on the platform and drove repeat purchasing behavior.

Amazon's implementation of try-before-you-buy (7-day delayed billing) illustrates the guarantee lever applied to physical products. At the point of 'payment', the buyer has already tried on the item; if they like it, their certainty of outcome is maximal. Hormozi contrasts this with the standard money-back guarantee, which he describes as having become table stakes for physical products, no longer differentiating on its own.

Amazon's product listings show 'Only 2 left' or 'Only 6 left' broken down by size to display scarcity at a granular level. Hormozi uses this as his primary example that scarcity is a deliberate, measurable conversion lever in e-commerce, not an accidental byproduct of inventory management.

practices.text: For physical products with complex usage (supplements, home health devices, appliances), create bonus instructional content: how to use the product, optimal timing, what to combine it with, how to avoid forgetting to use it. Package this as part of the offer, not as an afterthought.

When naming a physical product, embed the dream outcome explicitly in the product name so that the buyer whose job-to-be-done matches immediately self-identifies with the offer. Use search terms that buyers already use when naming products on Amazon or similar platforms.

Identify the distinct dream outcomes your product can fulfill, then create separate messaging and potentially separate listings or product variants for each avatar segment, rather than trying to serve all dream outcomes with a single undifferentiated message.

For e-commerce operators not selling on Amazon: study which of the eight value-equation levers (Dream Outcome, Likelihood, Time Delay, Effort/Sacrifice, Scarcity, Urgency, Guarantee, Bonus, Naming) your product listing currently implements, then prioritize closing the gaps where competitors who share your product have not yet invested.
